title: Gibraltar: Border fluidity, sovereignty and the new UK‑EU arrangement
label: 15 September 2026 · UK‑EU Agreement on Gibraltar
summary: The Chief Minister of Gibraltar, Hon Fabian Picardo, told the Lords’ European Affairs Committee why 96% of Gibraltarians backed the treaty with the EU, how it protects daily movement across the Gibraltar–Spain border, what it means for Gibraltar’s sovereignty, and how practical issues like customs, visas, taxation and residency will be handled. He said the deal is imperfect but necessary to keep people and goods flowing, that Gibraltar’s sovereignty hasn’t been weakened, and that provisional application from 15 July has so far worked though some operational tweaks are needed.

chapters.title: Why Gibraltarians overwhelmingly supported the treaty
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltarians backed the treaty because it protects daily life and work links with Spain and the EU while keeping Gibraltar British.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Fabian, thank you for joining us from Gibraltar. To begin, why did 96% of people there vote for the treaty, and how did the 2016 UK referendum affect Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Thanks. In 2016 the UK vote to leave the EU threatened Gibraltar’s economy and the easy cross-border life people take for granted. Many Gibraltarians rely on family and work links in southern Spain, and around 15,000 people cross the border into Gibraltar every day. People understood that Brexit could make all that harder, so they voted overwhelmingly to remain and later backed this deal that restores movement and trade while keeping Gibraltar British.

turns.speaker: Baroness Suttie
turns.text: So the treaty is mostly about practical daily life rather than a change of political control?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Exactly. It’s about keeping people moving and the economy functioning. It’s imperfect, but it’s what’s needed to prevent disruption to health care, public services and businesses.

chapters.title: How the border works under the treaty – visas, Schengen and EES explained
chapters.takeaway: The agreement keeps Gibraltar British but lets Schengen rules handle cross‑border travel in a way that aims to avoid big queues and protect jobs.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: You’ve said the European Court of Justice (the EU’s top court) can interpret EU rules applied under this deal. Doesn’t that threaten Gibraltar’s sovereignty?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: No. An analogy: when you join a club you agree the club’s referee interprets the club’s rules. Gibraltar chose to follow some EU rules for movement and goods, and the EU court interprets those EU rules so everyone uses the same legal meaning. That’s legal consistency, not a loss of sovereignty—the UK and Gibraltar kept full sovereignty over who governs the territory.

turns.speaker: The Duke of Wellington
turns.text: Did the UK change of government in 2024 slow the talks?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Both UK parties supported Gibraltar. The negotiations began earlier and continued across governments. A wider European security shift in 2025 also pushed parties to cooperate faster.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: How will individual refusals to enter Gibraltar actually work? Who decides and what happens to someone refused by one side but accepted by the other?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Gibraltar keeps the right to allow or refuse people from entering the territory—those are our immigration checks. Schengen checks (the passport-free area’s system) decide entry to the EU Schengen area. If Gibraltar lets someone into Gibraltar but Schengen refuses them, they can stay in Gibraltar only. If Gibraltar refuses but Schengen allows them, they can enter Schengen by a different exit route at Gibraltar airport but not go into Gibraltar. In short, checks are consecutive and separate.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: Any real cases so far where people fall between the two systems?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: In the first two months of provisional application we haven’t seen examples of someone admitted to Gibraltar but refused by Schengen. There have been some outright refusals to both systems, mostly where documentation was missing.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ashton of Upholland
turns.text: You mentioned the EES—what is that and why was provisional application needed?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: EES is the EU Entry/Exit System: a biometric database that records people entering and leaving Schengen. The July deadline for EES would have required massive on‑the‑spot checks and could have clogged the frontier. Because the treaty couldn’t be fully ratified before EES deadlines, the parties agreed to provisional application from 15 July so the new arrangements could operate while the formal ratification process finished. It avoids chaotic queues.

chapters.title: Sovereignty, courts and legal protections
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar’s political sovereignty remains British, but it has voluntarily accepted EU law in certain areas; dispute resolution by the EU court covers only those EU rules.

turns.speaker: Baroness Smith of Newnham
turns.text: You’ve insisted sovereignty wasn’t to be handed over. Has that been kept?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Yes. The UK and Gibraltar insisted on what we call the ‘double lock’ from the 2006 constitution: Gibraltar stays British and sovereignty hasn’t been transferred. We negotiated acceptance of specific EU rules for the practical relationship, but not sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: So the European Court of Justice (ECJ) can rule on EU law aspects—won’t that be a back‑door influence?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: The ECJ only interprets EU law that Gibraltar voluntarily agreed would apply for movement and certain goods. That’s the same model we had inside the EU: you accept a court’s role for the rules you choose to follow. It’s about legal clarity, not political control.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: What about trade deals like the CPTPP and new tech rules—will Gibraltar be forced to follow EU product rules like the AI product parts or Cyber Resilience Act?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Gibraltar’s economy is almost entirely services, not goods. The treaty covers physical things (people and goods) to keep movement fluid. For services, Gibraltar can follow the UK and take UK trade deals like CPTPP in services. There are grey areas where services and goods meet, but for core tech and service rules Gibraltar remains free to act with the UK unless we specifically signed EU product rules into the treaty.

chapters.title: Practical impacts: customs, tax, residency and the short‑term picture
chapters.takeaway: Provisional application has mostly worked, Gibraltar will fund a regional training fund itself, it keeps strong transparency on tax, and new local residency rules aim to protect Gibraltar’s small labour market.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell
turns.text: Who pays for the cooperation money and what’s it for?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Gibraltar will contribute and seek industry support. It’s not UK taxpayers funding this. The fund is for regional cohesion and training so the local job market has the people it needs. Initially it’ll be in the low millions of pounds and may grow.

turns.speaker: Lord Barrow
turns.text: How did Gibraltar’s parliament react and what’s the concordat you mentioned?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Parliament in Gibraltar voted unanimously to endorse the treaty. The concordat is a written agreement between the UK and Gibraltar spelling out who does what on the ground—who runs frontier checks, who pays for which duties—because it’s a UK treaty but Gibraltar executes most functions locally. That clarification was important and accepted in Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ashton of Upholland
turns.text: Has provisional application from 15 July revealed any persistent problems?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: We’ve seen some initial teething problems: customs procedures need consistent application on the EU side; port and airport layouts need tweaks to handle biometric EES enrolments at peaks; and one local fair once slowed truck flows. Truck numbers dipped briefly but are back up—fluidity overall is good and working.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: You said Gibraltar tightened its residency rules. Could that push young Brits out of your labour market?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: That concern comes from a misunderstanding. Very few young Brits casually come to work in Gibraltar today; our market is mainly local residents and cross‑border workers. We have about seven unemployed residents at moment—literally seven names—so labour is tight. New residency rules set a minimum earnings test (around £37,000) to keep residency manageable in a tiny territory. That’s our sovereign choice, not a treaty requirement.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: Do banks and services for British expats on the Costas still centre on Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: No. After Brexit most banking and mortgages moved to Spain or EU branches. People visiting from Spain often come to Gibraltar to shop or sightsee, but the old model of Costas expats doing their banking in Gibraltar has largely gone.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: You mentioned sanitary and phytosanitary rules (SPS). Could future UK‑EU SPS talks affect what food can move to Gibraltar from the UK?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Yes. Gibraltar currently follows EU rules for goods. If the UK reaches an SPS deal with the EU, that could make moving UK goods to Gibraltar easier. But any change will depend on wider UK‑EU agreement and what compromises are made there.

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: One final practical point: we were the first EU jurisdiction to introduce an open register of beneficial ownership of companies, ahead of many larger states. We’re committed to high transparency and meeting OECD/EU tax‑good‑governance standards, so treaty rules on tax transparency posed no problem for us.

chapters.title: Is this the final settlement and closing remarks
chapters.takeaway: The treaty solves the immediate practical problems and leaves sovereignty untouched, but future politics could reopen issues—overall it’s a pragmatic fix.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: Is the deal likely to settle things for the long term, or will more negotiations be needed?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: For daily fluidity and the UK‑EU relationship on Gibraltar it should be seen as settled. Politics can always reheat the issue, especially in election years, but legally and practically this agreement gives the clarity we needed. Sovereignty remains with the UK and Gibraltar keeps defending its right to self‑determination internationally.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Fabian, thank you for your time. Any final words?

turns.speaker: Fabian Picardo
turns.text: Just my thanks to the committee for interest in Gibraltar. I’ll be retiring in the coming months, so this may be my last appearance—I've enjoyed the collaboration and debate over the years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We wish you a happy and busy retirement. This evidence will help the Lords consider the treaty—thank you.
